Geometry and topology

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics
OurBigBook.com Words: 264k Articles: 5k
How much information about a shape do we need to keep? Euclidean geometry retains lengths and angles, allowing questions about the diagonal of a rectangle or the shortest route between two points. Topology retains the structure preserved by a homeomorphism, allowing questions about connectedness and whether a loop can shrink to a point, as recorded by the fundamental group. These are different levels of description of the same object.
For example, stretching a circle horizontally produces an ellipse. The stretching map and its inverse are continuous maps, so it gives a homeomorphism: the two curves have the same topology. It changes some Euclidean distances, however, so it is not an isometry. This distinction helps separate essential structure from a particular drawing, while explaining why measuring a shape requires more information than recognizing its topology.
The choice of geometry matters too. A Euclidean geometry triangle has interior angles summing to π, but a spherical triangle can have three right angles. Spherical geometry turns this apparent surprise into a measurement: the excess of the angle sum over π determines the area. Begin with the Pythagorean theorem for flat measurements, then compare the spherical triangle below to see curvature change the rules.

Cylinder (geometry)

Words: 286 Articles: 2
Geometry and topology OurBigBook.com
A cylinder is generated by translating a plane curve along parallel lines transverse to its plane. A circular cylinder uses a circle as its generating plane curve; it is right when the generators are perpendicular to that plane. The term can denote the lateral surface or, for a bounded portion with end caps, the enclosed solid. The circular cylinder curvature formulas describe the smooth lateral surface.

Geodesics on a generalized cylinder (z=F(y),u(y)=∫y1+F′(s)2​ds,u=ax+b)

Words: 108
Cylinder (geometry) OurBigBook.com
For a smooth surface obtained by translating the plane graph z=F(y) along the x direction, the induced metric is ds2=dx2+[1+F′(y)2]dy2. The transverse arc length coordinate u(y)=∫y1+F′(s)2​ds makes it ds2=dx2+du2. This is a local isometry to the Euclidean plane, extending the intrinsic flatness of a circular cylinder to arbitrary smooth generating graphs.
Its geodesics therefore lift to straight lines in (x,u) coordinates. Those that are graphs over x satisfy u=ax+b, while the additional family x=constant cannot be written as y(x). The same graph formula follows from the Beltrami identity for the arc-length integrand 1+[1+F′(y)2]y′2​. These straight lines are locally minimizing; on cylinders with a closed generating curve, global identifications can create several different winding paths between two points.

Optimal aspect ratios of closed cylinders (ℓ/a=2 at fixed area;ℓ/a=5​−1 inside a sphere)

Words: 121
Cylinder (geometry) OurBigBook.com
A closed circular cylinder of radius a>0 and length ℓ>0 has volume πa2ℓ and total surface area 2πa(a+ℓ), including both end disks. At fixed area A, Lagrange multipliers for maximizing the volume give ℓ=2a, hence
a=6πA​​,Vmax​=31​6πA3​​.
(1)
Equivalently, eliminate ℓ=A/(2πa)−a and maximize (A/2)a−πa3 on 0<a<A/(2π)​. The derivative changes from positive to negative at the displayed radius, and the volume tends to zero at both ends.
For a cylinder inscribed in a sphere of radius R, the constraint is a2+ℓ2/4=R2. Maximizing a2+aℓ by Lagrange multipliers gives ℓ2+2aℓ=4a2, so the positive aspect ratio is ℓ/a=5​−1. It is independent of R. With q=ℓ/a, the area is 2πR2(1+q)/(1+q2/4); differentiating this expression confirms the unique maximum on q>0.

Parametric equation

Words: 39
Geometry and topology OurBigBook.com
A parametric equation expresses coordinates as functions of one or more independent parameters. For example, x=cost, y=sint describes a circle; multiple parameters describe surfaces. A smooth curve is a differentiable single-parameter realization. A reparametrization changes the parameter without changing the geometric image.

Embedding

Words: 38
Geometry and topology OurBigBook.com
An embedding identifies one mathematical structure with a structure-preserving copy inside another. In topology it is a homeomorphism onto its image with the subspace topology; an algebraic embedding is an injective homomorphism. A smooth embedding additionally has injective differential everywhere, so its image is an embedded submanifold.

Pencil (geometry)

Words: 43
Geometry and topology OurBigBook.com
A pencil is a one-parameter linear family of geometric objects. For linearly independent homogeneous polynomials F,G of equal degree, sF+tG=0, indexed by [s:t]∈P1, is a pencil of plane curves or hypersurfaces. Lines through a fixed point give a simple example; a pencil of plane curves specializes the general construction.

Spherical geometry

Words: 2k Articles: 9
Geometry and topology OurBigBook.com
Spherical geometry studies lengths and angles measured along the surface of a sphere, rather than through its interior. It is a useful model whenever travel is constrained to a round surface. Its straightest paths are great circle arcs: they are geodesics, even though they appear curved in the surrounding Euclidean space. Two distinct great circles meet at an antipodal pair, so the parallel-line picture of Euclidean geometry does not apply.
For a sphere of radius R>0, write two positions as Ru,Rv, with u,v unit vectors. Their shorter surface route has great-circle distance
d=Rarccos(u⋅v),
(2)
where the dot product gives the central angle in radians. The straight chord through the surrounding Euclidean space instead has length 2Rsin(d/(2R)). For a quarter-circle separation these are πR/2≈1.571R and 2​R≈1.414R: specifying which distance we mean has a measurable effect. On the unit sphere, R=1 and great-circle distance equals the central angle.
Consider the spherical triangle with vertices (R,0,0), (0,R,0) and (0,0,R), joined by the shorter great circle arcs. Each side has length πR/2. At each vertex the two outgoing tangent vectors point along the other coordinate axes and are orthogonal, so all three interior angles are π/2. This is the positive coordinate octant of the sphere, not a flat triangle drawn inside it.
For a convex minor spherical triangle with interior angles α,β,γ in radians, the spherical excess formula states
A=R2(α+β+γ−π).
(3)
Our octant therefore has area R2(3π/2−π)=πR2/2. Independently, eight congruent octants partition the sphere, giving 4πR2/8 again. Thus angles alone determine area when R is fixed, unlike Euclidean geometry, where similar triangles can have arbitrarily different areas. The Gauss-Bonnet theorem explains the connection: the sphere's constant Gaussian curvature 1/R2 times the area equals this excess. For spherical triangles whose area is small compared with R2, the excess is small, recovering the familiar flat picture.

Convex regular spherical polygon (nn−2​π<α<π)

Words: 62
Spherical geometry OurBigBook.com
A nondegenerate convex regular spherical n-gon contained in an open hemisphere has equal interior angles α in the displayed interval. The spherical excess formula gives area nα−(n−2)π>0. Conversely, put equally spaced vertices at colatitude t∈(0,π/2) around a pole. Dividing each central triangle in half gives cot(α/2)=costtan(π/n) by the spherical law of cosines. As t increases, the angle ranges continuously from the Euclidean limiting angle to π.

Spherical circle (C(r)=2πRsin(r/R))

Words: 65
Spherical geometry OurBigBook.com
On a sphere of radius R, a spherical circle of radius r∈(0,πR) is the locus at spherical distance r from its center. Its polar angle about that center is r/R, so parametrization by longitude has speed Rsin(r/R). Its circumference is therefore 2πRsin(r/R). For small r, this is 2πr−πr3/(3R2)+O(r5), with the deficit determined by the sphere's positive Gaussian curvature.

Spherical geometry OurBigBook.com
Spherical trigonometry calculates the sides and interior angles of spherical triangles using trigonometric functions. Its sides must be shorter great circle arcs, which are geodesics on a round sphere. A curve at constant nonzero latitude does not qualify. The spherical law of sines and spherical law of cosines play the roles of the familiar flat-triangle rules, but account for the sphere's curvature.
Use uppercase A,B,C both for the vertices and for their interior angles, and lowercase a,b,c for the opposite angular sides. For example, a is the central angle subtended by the arc from B to C. On a sphere of radius R, its physical arc length is ℓa​=Ra when a is in radians; similarly ℓb​=Rb and ℓc​=Rc. Only on the unit sphere do the angular and physical side lengths have the same numerical values. See J. B. Tatum, Celestial Mechanics, chapter 3, section 3.5: great-circle sides and angular units.
One useful application of spherical trigonometry is finding great-circle distance from spherical coordinates. Write a unit vector as u(ϕ,λ)=(cosϕcosλ,cosϕsinλ,sinϕ), where ϕ is latitude and λ is the equatorial azimuth, or longitude, measured from a chosen reference direction. The dot product of two such unit vectors gives
cosδ=sinϕ1​sinϕ2​+cosϕ1​cosϕ2​cos(λ2​−λ1​),d=Rδ.
(4)
Here δ∈[0,π] is the central angle and d is the great-circle distance. The same identity follows from the spherical law of cosines by adding the north pole as the third vertex, with angular sides π/2−ϕ1​ and π/2−ϕ2​. This connects spherical geometry to position calculations in astronomy and to navigation on a spherical model of Earth. Choosing the surface model matters: Paula Neeley and Anthony Narkawicz, Map Projection Induced Variations in Locations of Polygon Geofence Edges, NASA/TM-2017-219675 (2017), sections 2-3 distinguishes spherical and ellipsoidal geodesics and gives this coordinate identity.
For a toy example, put two points at latitude 30∘, with equatorial azimuths −60∘ and 60∘. The great-circle distance and the arc length along constant latitude are
d=Rarccos(41​+43​cos120∘)=Rarccos(−1/8)≈1.696124R,ℓparallel​=Rcos30∘32π​≈1.813799R.
(5)
The great circle takes a shorter route by bending towards the pole in these spherical coordinates. To locate its highest latitude, the endpoint unit vectors are p=(3​/4,−3/4,1/2) and q=(3​/4,3/4,1/2). Their great circle lies in the plane through the origin with z=2x/3​. On its shorter arc, the maximum latitude occurs at y=0 and is arctan(2/3​)≈49.106605∘. Thus a geodesic can change latitude substantially even when its endpoints have equal latitude. These are lengths on an ideal sphere; the example illustrates the geometry rather than specifying an actual flight route.
Historically, spherical trigonometry was prominent in teaching as well as in astronomy. John Conway and Alex Ryba note its presence in early twentieth-century school textbooks in Remembering spherical trigonometry, The Mathematical Gazette 100(547), March 2016, pages 1-8, DOI 10.1017/mag.2016.3. Their introductory observation documents that teaching history; it does not identify a single inventor of the spherical law of sines or spherical law of cosines.

The sines of sides refer to central angles, so a physical side length ℓa​ on a sphere of radius R must enter as sin(ℓa​/R). All six angles lie in (0,π), and the denominators are positive. The reciprocal form, sina/sinA=sinb/sinB=sinc/sinC, is equivalent. This is Tatum's sine formula, equation 3.5.1, in Celestial Mechanics, section 3.5: spherical sine and cosine formulas.
A short proof explains the symmetry of the spherical law of sines. Let u,v,w be the vertex unit vectors at A,B,C. At u, the outgoing unit tangent vectors towards v,w are tB​=(v−coscu)/sinc and tC​=(w−cosbu)/sinb. Their angle is A, so the magnitude of their cross product is sinA. Since both tangent vectors are orthogonal to u, the scalar triple product obeys
∣u⋅(v×w)∣=sinbsincsinA=sincsinasinB=sinasinbsinC.
(7)
Dividing by sinasinbsinc proves the spherical law of sines. Its beauty is that the same three-dimensional scalar triple product can be calculated at any vertex, producing all three ratios at once.
For the spherical triangle worked out under the spherical law of cosines, A=90∘, b=c=60∘ and cosa=1/4. Hence sina=15​/4, and the spherical law of sines gives

The spherical law of cosines, using the known three sides, gives cosB=1/5​>0 and selects 63.434949∘; likewise C=B. When only two sides and an opposite angle are given, two distinct valid spherical triangles can remain. A cosine relation resolves an inverse sine branch only when enough additional data are known; it does not make every ambiguous data set unique.

Reflections in the sides of a spherical triangle of angles π/p,π/q,π/r generate a finite group when its images tessellate the sphere. The triangle area is π(1/p+1/q+1/r−1) by the spherical excess formula. Label its three vertex types and continue those labels across each reflected side; they are consistent around every vertex and, because the sphere is simply connected, globally. The generated group preserves these labels, so a chamber stabilizer fixes all three vertices and is trivial. Dividing sphere area by chamber area gives its order. Up to permutation the possibilities are (2,2,n) for n≥2, and (2,3,3),(2,3,4),(2,3,5), of orders 4n,24,48,120.

Minkowski addition (A+B)

Words: 1k Articles: 4
Convex geometry OurBigBook.com
The Minkowski sum of subsets A,B of a vector space collects the result of vector addition for every possible pair:
A+B={a+b:a∈A, b∈B}=⋃b∈B​(A+b).
(15)
Think of fixing a point b of B, making a translation of the whole of A by b, and then taking the union of these copies over every b∈B. The points of B specify displacement vectors; they need not be the centre of a shape. Minkowski addition applies to nonconvex sets too. It is different from set union: for A=B={0,1} on the real line, A∪B={0,1} but A+B={0,1,2}.
For axis-aligned rectangles in the Euclidean plane, the coordinate intervals add separately:
([0,a]×[0,b])+([0,c]×[0,d])=[0,a+c]×[0,b+d],a,b,c,d>0.
(16)
Every coordinate between 0 and a+c can be split into one coordinate in [0,a] and another in [0,c], and likewise for the vertical coordinate. Thus a 2×1 rectangle plus a 1×2 rectangle gives a 3×3 square of area 9, although the two input areas total only 4. The Minkowski sum adds possible displacements, so its area need not be the sum of input areas.
For closed Euclidean disks Dr​={x∈R2:∥x∥≤r} centred at the origin, the triangle inequality gives Dr​+Ds​⊆Dr+s​. Conversely, if r+s>0, split any x∈Dr+s​ as x=rx/(r+s)+sx/(r+s). Therefore Dr​+Ds​=Dr+s​, including the case r=s=0. Disks of radii 1 and 2 give a disk of radius 3, with areas π,4π,9π. For disks with centres u,v, the resulting centre is u+v. These two examples lead to the root-of-area comparison in the Brunn-Minkowski theorem.
Minkowski addition is commutative and associative because vector addition is. Its identity is the singleton {0}, and A+∅=∅. For displacement vectors u,v and t>0, translations and uniform dilations satisfy
(A+u)+(B+v)=(A+B)+(u+v),t(A+B)=tA+tB,
(17)
where tA={ta:a∈A} uses scalar multiplication. A Minkowski sum of convex sets is convex: a line segment between a1​+b1​ and a2​+b2​ is obtained by adding the corresponding points of the line segments in A and B. Closure requires care; see sum of two closed sets need not be closed and sum of a compact set and a closed set.

Minkowski addition for collision detection (Cobs​=O+(−R))

Minkowski addition OurBigBook.com
Suppose a robot occupies a closed set R⊆Rn relative to its chosen reference point, and a closed obstacle occupies O. Keep the robot's orientation fixed and allow only translations. At reference position q, its occupied set is q+R. If touching counts as collision, the forbidden positions in this configuration space are exactly
q∈Cobs​​⟺(q+R)∩O=∅⟺q+r=o for some r∈R, o∈O⟺q∈O+(−R),−R={−r:r∈R}.​
(18)
The minus sign reflects the robot through its reference origin: solving q+r=o gives q=o−r. Thus collision checking for a moving shape becomes checking whether one point lies in a fixed Minkowski sum. Steven M. LaValle derives this translational configuration space construction in Planning Algorithms, section 4.3.2, equation 4.37 and Example 4.13.
For a concrete toy example, take the robot rectangle R=[0,2]×[0,1] with its reference point at the lower-left corner, and obstacle rectangle O=[4,6]×[2,4]. Their collision region is the rectangle
O+(−R)=[2,6]×[1,4],λ2​(Cobs​)=4⋅3=12.
(19)
For example, q=(3,3/2) is forbidden: q+R=[3,5]×[3/2,5/2] meets O in [4,5]×[2,5/2], of area 1/2. At q=(2,1) there is just corner contact, which our convention also forbids. Using O+R=[4,8]×[2,5] instead would wrongly miss both reference positions. Only when R=−R, as for an origin-centred disk, does the reflection leave the robot set unchanged.
The same calculation handles bounded additive uncertainty. If the actual reference position is q+e for any e∈E, the union of possible occupied sets is q+(E+R). There exists an allowed error causing contact exactly when
q∈O+(−(E+R))=O+(−R)+(−E).
(20)
Consequently avoiding this set guarantees avoidance for every e∈E in this model. For E=[−ε,ε]2, the example's forbidden region becomes [2−ε,6+ε]×[1−ε,4+ε], with area (4+2ε)(3+2ε). Here −E=E because the error bounds are symmetric; a one-sided error set must still be negated. This is a worst-case geometric bound, not a probability of collision. Rotating the robot requires an orientation-dependent Minkowski sum for each orientation.

Brunn-Minkowski theorem (λn​(A+B)1/n≥λn​(A)1/n+λn​(B)1/n)

Words: 421
Minkowski addition OurBigBook.com
Let n≥1 and let A,B⊆Rn be nonempty Lebesgue measurable sets with finite Lebesgue measures. Assume that A+B is also a Lebesgue measurable set; its measure may be infinite. Then
λn​(A+B)1/n≥λn​(A)1/n+λn​(B)1/n.
(21)
Here λn​ denotes n-dimensional Lebesgue measure in Euclidean space. Nonempty compact sets and nonempty open sets of finite measure satisfy the measurability assumptions. Measurability of arbitrary summands alone does not guarantee measurability of their Minkowski sum. The theorem does not require convexity. See R. J. Gardner, The Brunn-Minkowski Inequality (2002), Theorem 4.1 and the following remarks.
The nth root converts a volume into a quantity that scales like a length: uniform dilation gives λn​(tA)1/n=tλn​(A)1/n for t>0. In the Euclidean plane the theorem compares square roots of areas, not the areas themselves. For the two rectangles above it reads 3≥2​+2​=22​. Equivalently their sum has area 9≥8. For the two disks, it reads 3π​=π​+2π​, an equality. These are exact geometric examples, not measured data.
Applying the theorem to the scaled sets gives, whenever that sum is a Lebesgue measurable set,
λn​((1−t)A+tB)1/n≥(1−t)λn​(A)1/n+tλn​(B)1/n,0<t<1.
(22)
For convex bodies, this means the root-volume of the interpolated shape lies above the straight line between the input root-volumes. In fact t↦λn​((1−t)A+tB)1/n is a concave function on [0,1]: convexity gives sA+tA=(s+t)A for s,t≥0, so interpolating two intermediate shapes gives another intermediate shape and the same inequality applies. The beauty is that no particular boundary shape appears in the bound: possible pointwise displacements force a minimum amount of space.
For convex bodies A,B, equality holds exactly when they are homothetic convex bodies, meaning B=v+sA for some vector v and s>0. This equality qualification is part of the Brunn-Minkowski theorem for convex bodies. [ref] For positive-sided axis-aligned rectangles, the comparison can be checked directly:
(a+c)(b+d)−(ab​+cd​)2=(ad​−bc​)2≥0.
(23)
Equality requires ad=bc: the rectangles must have the same aspect ratio. Our 2×1 and 1×2 rectangles do not. All positive-radius disks are homothetic convex bodies, explaining their equality.
Do not apply that equality criterion without its hypotheses. If A={a}, its Lebesgue measure is zero and A+B is a translation of B, so equality holds even for nonconvex B. Also, changing a summand on a null set can change the measure of its Minkowski sum: in one dimension, A=[0,1]∪{3} and B=[0,1] both have measure 1, but A+B=[0,2]∪[3,4] has measure 3. Removing the single extra point restores equality with sum measure 2. Thus merely being equal almost everywhere to homothetic convex bodies is not a sufficient equality test for arbitrary sets.
The Brunn-Minkowski theorem also bounds the collision-region volume: for positive-volume compact sets O,R, reflection preserves Lebesgue measure, so λn​(O+(−R))1/n≥λn​(O)1/n+λn​(R)1/n. In the toy collision example this gives area at least (2+2​)2=6+42​≈11.657, compared with the exact area 12. A lower bound alone does not identify safe reference positions; the actual Minkowski sum supplies those.

This map is not a linear map with respect to the displayed origins, because T(0,0)=(1,−2) rather than zero. It also is not a Euclidean similarity: AB has length 2 and A′B′ has length 4, while the right angle at A becomes 45∘. Its determinant is 2, so it doubles planar area. These metric changes explain why affine geometry studies straightness, incidence and weighted points rather than treating every transformation as an isometry.
The linear part is an invertible matrix, giving the concise inverse T−1(u,v)=((u−v−3)/2,v+2). More generally an affine map is bijective exactly when its linear part of an affine map is bijective. Between equal finite-dimensional spaces, this means an invertible matrix; the translation cannot repair a loss of rank of a linear map.

Glue the corresponding edge of a copy labelled g to its mate in the copy labelled gAk​. Left multiplication of labels defines the T action. A vertex cycle of a paired polygon has angle sum θj​ and accumulated gluing word Cj​∈T of order qj​; above it lie ∣T∣/qj​ vertices, each of cone angle qj​θj​. The action is free away from vertices, and the vertex stabilizers are conjugates of ⟨Cj​⟩. If the base cone has integer order mj​=2π/θj​ and qj​∣mj​, this is an orbifold covering, with lifted cone order mj​/qj​. The lift is smooth exactly when qj​=mj​.

The chosen sector and its branch must be identified by an interior test point; merely squaring an arbitrary boundary-straightening map need not be injective on the intended domain. A Cayley transform then gives a conformal bijection to a disc.

Conformal geometry studies a metric tensor only up to multiplication by a nowhere-zero positive scalar function on a real slice. A conformal class determines angles in Riemannian signature and null directions in Lorentzian signature. The complexified flat four-dimensional conformal geometry is encoded by the Klein quadric, whose incidence relation describes null separation.

An equivalence class of Riemannian metrics under multiplication by positive smooth functions. Such rescalings preserve angles. On an oriented smooth surface, a conformal structure is equivalent to a complex structure, with local holomorphic coordinates in which its metrics are positive multiples of dx2+dy2.

A conformal compactification realizes a noncompact metric space as a dense open subset of a compact space whose metric on that subset is conformally related to the original one. Its smoothness and boundary interpretation depend on the example. Conformal compactification of Euclidean space adds one point to four-space; Projective Minkowski compactification adds a null cone. A regular null-boundary conformal completion and a projective compactification need not have the same global topology or causal covering convention.
Conformal boundary (g​=Ω2g,Ω=0,dΩ=0)
Words: 80
Conformal compactification OurBigBook.com
A boundary obtained by extending the rescaled metric g​=Ω2g smoothly and nondegenerately to a hypersurface on which Ω vanishes with nonzero derivative. Its causal character is measured using the extended Lorentzian metric, not the divergent physical metric. In signature (+−−−), a timelike normal makes the boundary spacelike, a spacelike normal makes it timelike, and a null normal makes it null. These cases lead to different causal and initial-value properties. The conformal cylinder of two-dimensional de Sitter spacetime has spacelike past/future boundaries; the conformal strip of two-dimensional anti-de Sitter spacetime has two timelike boundaries.

In the Klein quadric description, the compact space is the projectivized real null cone of signature (1,5). It differs topologically from Minkowski conformal compactification.

Both are real slices of the same complex Klein quadric, which permits local analytic continuation without equating their global real topologies.
In affine cone coordinates [U,V,t,x] with 2UV+t2−∣x∣2=0 and U=1, the substitution is represented on the complex quadric by the rational map [U,V,t,x]↦[U2,UV+t2,iUt,Ux]. Connected space

Words: 2k Articles: 18
Geometry and topology OurBigBook.com
A topological space X is connected when it has no separation of a topological space: no partition of a set into two nonempty open subsets U,V satisfying
X=U∪V,U∩V=∅.
(30)
Here the union covers all of X, and the intersection is the empty set, so no point belongs to both pieces. For a subset X of a larger topological space, "open" means open in the subspace topology: each piece is the intersection of X with an ambient open set. Both pieces must be open; merely dividing a drawing into two colours does not establish a separation of a topological space. [ref]
For example, the closed interval I=[0,1] with its usual subspace topology from the real line is connected. The proposed split [0,1/2)∪[1/2,1] fails: the second subset is not open in I, since every neighbourhood of 1/2 in I contains points less than 1/2. More generally, a connected subset of the real line is precisely a real interval. In contrast, for the union
D=[−2,−1]∪[1,2],U=D∩(−3,0)=[−2,−1],V=D∩(0,3)=[1,2],
(31)
the open intervals (−3,0) and (0,3) exhibit U,V as nonempty open subsets in the subspace topology of D. Their intersection is empty and their union is D, so D is not connected. Although U,V are closed intervals in the real line, they are also open within D.
Why is connectedness useful? A continuous image of a connected space is connected: a proposed separation of a topological space in the image would pull back through the continuous map to a forbidden separation of a topological space in its source. Thus a continuous map from a real interval to the real line cannot skip values between two attained values. This is the intermediate value theorem. For a computed example, the continuous function f(x)=x2 on [0,1] has image [0,1]; the value 1/2 occurs at x=1/2​≈0.707107. Connectedness guarantees an input attaining that value even when we have no formula for it.
Path connectedness is a stronger condition: it supplies a continuous path between every pair of points. The topologist's sine curve below shows that a connected space need not be a path-connected space.

Immediately afterwards its first coordinate x(t)>0 approaches zero and its second coordinate is sin(1/x(t)). The intermediate value theorem forces the first coordinate to pass through inputs of both displayed types arbitrarily close to that departure time. The second coordinate therefore takes both values 1 and −1 arbitrarily close to that time, contradicting continuity. [ref]

Connected component (Cx​)

Connected space OurBigBook.com
A connected component of a topological space X is a nonempty connected subset that is maximal under subset inclusion. If C is a connected component and C⊆D⊆X with D a connected subset, then D=C. Maximality means that no larger connected subset contains C; it does not mean largest cardinality among all connected subsets.
For example, the connected components of [−2,2]∖{0} in the usual subspace topology of the real line are [−2,0) and (0,2]. Each is a real interval, and no connected subset of the real line can meet both without containing the missing point 0. For the finite set {−2,0,2} in the same subspace topology, the three connected components are its singleton sets.
Every point x∈X lies in exactly one connected component, constructed by taking the union
Cx​=⋃{A⊆X:x∈A and A is connected}.
(35)
All members contain x, so their union is connected by connected union with a connected hub. The union includes every connected subset through x, so it is maximal. Equivalently, define
x∼y⟺some connected subset of X contains both x and y.
(36)
This is an equivalence relation: singleton sets give reflexivity, symmetry is immediate, and two connected subsets sharing the middle point have a connected union, giving transitivity. The equivalence classes are precisely the connected components. They form a partition of a set: they cover X and any two are either equal or disjoint.[ref]
Every nonempty connected subset lies within one connected component. Moreover, every connected component is closed in X: closure of a connected set makes its closure connected, and maximality forces that closure to equal the original connected component. A connected component need not be open. For example, in S={0}∪{1/n:n=1,2,…} with its usual subspace topology from the real line, all connected components are singleton sets, but {0} is not open: every neighbourhood of 0 in S contains some 1/n.[ref]

The numerator is the residual of the plane equation, not yet a length: its size depends on the chosen normal vector. Dividing by that vector's Euclidean norm removes this arbitrary scale.

Why is the perpendicular route shortest? Let q be the closest point on a plane and r any other point on it. The displacement p−q is orthogonal to q−r, so the Pythagorean theorem gives

Equality holds only for r=q. This is the closest-point principle of orthogonal decomposition, applied after a translation of an affine plane to its direction linear subspace.[ref]
The formula is useful whenever the deviation from a flat reference should be measured geometrically. A raw linear equation residual cannot be compared across arbitrary equation scalings; a perpendicular distance can. The same reasoning works for a hyperplane in any finite-dimensional Euclidean space, with the appropriate number of coordinates.

Geometry and topology OurBigBook.com
A topological space X is path-connected if, for every a,b∈X, there is a continuous map
γ:[0,1]⟶X,γ(0)=a,γ(1)=b.
(48)
This continuous path must stay within X for its entire duration. Its parameter need not represent physical time, and continuity does not require a derivative or finite arc length. [ref]
In the closed interval [0,1], any a,b are joined by γ(t)=(1−t)a+tb. For a=1/4 and b=3/4, this becomes γ(t)=1/4+t/2, so γ(0)=1/4, γ(1/2)=1/2, and γ(1)=3/4. All its values stay in [0,1]. In the union D=[−2,−1]∪[1,2], however, a continuous path from −1 to 1 would attain 0 by the intermediate value theorem, although 0∈/D. Thus D is not path-connected.
Every path-connected space is a connected space. Proof outline: if X=U∪V admitted a separation of a topological space, choose a∈U and b∈V. A continuous path between them would have nonempty open inverse images γ−1(U),γ−1(V) with empty intersection and union [0,1]. This contradicts the connectedness of that closed interval.
The converse fails: the topologist's sine curve is connected but has two path components. Path connectedness is useful when we need an actual continuous path of allowed positions, rather than only the absence of a separation of a topological space. For instance, when modelling allowed positions as a topological space, membership in the same path component answers whether one can move continuously between two positions while remaining in that topological space.

In three-dimensional Euclidean space, a Cartesian equation of a plane fixes one linear equation n⋅x=d, with a nonzero normal vector n. The two free directions are orthogonal to n. A plane extends indefinitely; a rectangular patch in a drawing marks only part of it, and does not define an edge of the plane.
For example, the plane 2x−y+2z=3 contains a=(1,1,1). The vectors u=(1,2,0) and v=(0,2,1) are linearly independent and satisfy (2,−1,2)⋅u=(2,−1,2)⋅v=0. Hence its points are exactly (1+s,1+2s+2t,1+t): substitution gives 2x−y+2z=3 for every real s,t, and every solution has s=x−1, t=z−1.
The description separates position from direction. A translation of the plane changes a and possibly d, while retaining its parallel directions. A plane through the origin is a linear subspace; the displayed example is not, since the zero vector fails its linear equation. This distinction matters when applying orthogonal projection: subtract an anchor point before projecting onto the direction linear subspace.
Historically, Euclid's Euclid's Elements by Euclid, Book I Definition 7, describes a plane surface through the straight lines lying on it. David E. Joyce's accompanying guide notes that this older use can include a bounded square or circular figure. That usage differs from the whole unbounded affine subspace used here.[ref]

In three-dimensional Euclidean space, a nonzero normal vector n=(a,b,c) determines the plane equation
ax+by+cz=d.

For a point a0​ on the plane, d=n⋅a0​, so the equivalent point-normal form is n⋅(x−a0​)=0. The difference of any two points on the plane is orthogonal to n, directly explaining its role as a normal vector.
Multiplying a,b,c,d by the same nonzero scalar preserves the set of solutions. Thus 2x−y+2z=3 and −6x+3y−6z=−9 describe the same plane. Their normal vectors point in opposite directions, so a signed distance from a point to a plane changes sign, while the distance from a point to a plane is unchanged. If a=b=c=0, the linear equation describes either all of space when d=0, or the empty set when d=0; it does not select a plane.

Product topology

Words: 2k Articles: 23
Geometry and topology OurBigBook.com
The product topology turns separate observations into a notion of closeness: a basic test checks finitely many coordinates, with a separate tolerance in each. For an index set I and topological spaces Xi​, the underlying Cartesian product and its coordinate projection maps are
X=∏i∈I​Xi​={(xi​)i∈I​:xi​∈Xi​},πi​:X→Xi​,πi​(x)=xi​.
(56)
The product topology is the coarsest topology making every πi​ a continuous map.[ref]
The Cartesian product specifies which points exist; the product topology specifies their neighborhoods. Finite observations motivate its finite-coordinate basis for the product topology, while convergence in a product space and continuity into a product space explain why it is useful. The compactness result for this construction is Tychonoff's theorem.

Finite-coordinate basis for the product topology (B(F,U)=⋂i∈F​πi−1​(Ui​))

Words: 262 Articles: 1
Product topology OurBigBook.com
For a finite set F⊆I and open sets Ui​⊆Xi​ for i∈F, the sets
B(F,U)=⋂i∈F​πi−1​(Ui​)=∏i∈I​Vi​,Vi​={Ui​Xi​​i∈F,i∈/F​
(57)
form a basis of a topology for the product topology. The empty set intersection is X. Each basic open set is a cylinder set; all coordinates outside F are free. Arbitrary open sets are unions of these basic tests and need not themselves depend on one fixed finite collection of coordinates.[ref]
Why finitely many? Any topology making the projection maps continuous must contain their preimages of open sets, and hence finite set intersections of those preimages. Taking arbitrary unions supplies exactly the product topology. Intersecting two basic cylinder sets still restricts only the finite union of their coordinate sets.

Open rectangles in a finite product

Words: 152
Finite-coordinate basis for the product topology OurBigBook.com
On two copies of the real line with their usual topologies, let U=(1,2) and V=(2,4). The coordinate projection maps give
π1−1​(U)=U×R,π2−1​(V)=R×V,π1−1​(U)∩π2−1​(V)=U×V.
(58)
The first two open sets are unbounded strips; their set intersection is an open rectangle. The point (1.4,3) passes both coordinate tests, whereas (2,3) fails the first because the endpoint 2 is excluded.
Every point of an open set in the Euclidean plane has such an open rectangle around it inside that open set. Conversely, every open rectangle contains a small Euclidean ball around each of its points. Thus the product topology here is the usual metric topology of the Euclidean plane. With finitely many factors all coordinates may be restricted; on an infinite Cartesian product a basic cylinder set must leave all but finitely many factors free.

Convergence in a product space (x(n)→x⟺∀i∈I, πi​(x(n))→πi​(x))

Words: 362 Articles: 1
Product topology OurBigBook.com
For arbitrary topological spaces Xi​, an index set I, a sequence x(n)∈∏i​Xi​, and a point x in that Cartesian product, convergence in a product space to x in the product topology is equivalent to coordinatewise convergence in every factor. No countability or Hausdorff assumption on the factors is needed. For a product space of copies of the real line, regarding each point as a function I→R identifies this with pointwise convergence.
Proof outline: the forward implication follows because each projection map is continuous. Conversely, given a basic neighborhood B(F,U) of x, each of its finitely many coordinate tests holds for all n≥Ni​. Taking N=maxi∈F​Ni​ makes all tests hold simultaneously; if F is empty, any threshold works. This proves eventual membership in every neighborhood, rather than only in a sampled collection of cylinders. The same equivalence holds for nets: a directed set supplies a common upper bound for finitely many thresholds. Sequences alone need not characterize the whole topology of an arbitrary product space.

Let N={1,2,…} and give each factor of RN the usual topology of the real line. The familiar standard basis vectors extend to unit sequences en​ with (en​)j​=1 when j=n and zero otherwise. Their finite linear combinations are exactly the finitely supported sequences, rather than all of RN.
For every fixed coordinate j, (en​)j​=0 for all n>j. Therefore en​→0 in the product topology. More directly, any basic cylinder set B(F,U) containing zero contains every en​ with n>max(F∪{0}): all of its tested coordinates are then zero. The moving unit entry escapes every fixed finite collection of observations.
In the l-infinity sequence space of bounded real sequences, however,
∥en​−0∥∞​=supj≥1​∣(en​)j​∣=1.
(59)
Thus the same sequence does not converge to zero in the supremum norm. Here the comparison is between the subspace topology inherited from the product topology and the norm topology on ℓ∞. The supremum norm is not a finite-valued norm on all of RN, which also contains unbounded sequences. In the box topology on RN, the neighborhood ∏j≥1​(−1/2,1/2) of zero excludes every en​, so en​ is not a convergent sequence with limit zero there either.

Product topology OurBigBook.com
The box topology on ∏i∈I​Xi​ has a basis of a topology consisting of all Cartesian products ∏i​Ui​ with every Ui​ an open set in Xi​; infinitely many coordinates may be restricted. It contains the product topology and agrees with it for finite I.[ref]
For copies of the usual real line, the box topology is strictly finer when I=N. The box W=∏j≥1​(−1/2,1/2) is not an open set in the product topology: a basic cylinder set containing zero leaves some coordinate j unrestricted, so it contains ej​∈/W. This is a construction for every finite coordinate set, not evidence from testing a finite prefix.

a finite set intersection of open sets in Y. This gives continuity on every basic test. It explains, for example, why t↦(t,t2,t3,…) from the real line to RN is continuous in the product topology: each coordinate is a polynomial function. The general coordinate criterion fails for the box topology, where infinitely many preimages can be required at once. Trigonometric functions turn an angle into a coordinate or a ratio of lengths. Start at (1,0) on the unit circle and rotate counterclockwise through θ radians: the resulting point is

The cosine records horizontal position and the sine records vertical position. This definition continues around the whole circle, including negative angles, so the signs encode direction rather than requiring a separate rule for each right triangle.
The unit circle picture explains why these functions are useful beyond measuring triangles. The two coordinates of a point rotating at constant angular speed are periodic functions. Scaling the radius to A and using θ=ωt+ϕ gives x=Acos(ωt+ϕ) and y=Asin(ωt+ϕ). A circular motion becomes two simple repeating traces, connecting Euclidean geometry, simple harmonic motion, and Fourier series.
For an acute angle in a right triangle, rescaling its hypotenuse to one recovers the familiar ratios: sine is opposite side divided by hypotenuse, and cosine is adjacent side divided by hypotenuse. The tangent function is their ratio, tanθ=sinθ/cosθ, wherever the denominator is nonzero; the secant function, cosecant, and cotangent give the other reciprocal ratios.
The same names extend to complex numbers through the complex exponential:
cosz=2eiz+e−iz​,sinz=2ieiz−e−iz​.

These definitions agree with the circle interpretation for real angles. For complex arguments, the values need not lie between −1 and 1; the literal circle-coordinate picture is restricted to real arguments. [ref]

Words: 145
Trigonometric function OurBigBook.com
For every real angle θ,

It is the equation of the unit circle written in terms of its sine and cosine coordinates. For an acute angle, dividing the Pythagorean theorem by the square of the hypotenuse gives the same relation in a right triangle. The circle interpretation explains why it remains true outside that first-quadrant triangle.
For example, if sinθ=3/5, the identity gives cos2θ=16/25, so cosθ is either 4/5 or −4/5. The sign needs the angle's location: it is positive in the first quadrant and negative in the second. Thus the identity determines the magnitude of the missing coordinate without determining the direction.
The relation is useful for eliminating one squared trigonometric function, checking that a coordinate pair has unit length, and checking that the columns of a rotation matrix are unit vectors. It also holds for complex arguments under the complex exponential definitions, although then the squares are algebraic squares rather than squared moduli.

In three dimensions the mean occupied fraction scales as Na3/Rg3​∝(Rg​/a)df​−3. A smaller df​ therefore describes a more tenuous large cluster; a compact constant-density object has df​=3. A cover by Nδ​(E) balls implies ∣Eδ​∣≲n​δnNδ​(E) for the open δ-neighborhood. Conversely, a maximal separated subset gives the reverse comparison up to fixed changes of scale. This connects small-scale covering counts with neighborhood Lebesgue measure.

The open diamond {∣x−1/2∣+∣y∣<1/2} is an open set condition witness: its eight image diamonds have disjoint interiors and lie within it. Hence 8(1/4)s=1, giving Hausdorff dimension 3/2. This permits the closures to meet. For the invariant compact set, this separation makes its Hausdorff dimension equal to the similarity exponent s defined by ∑i​cis​=1, where ci​ are the contraction ratios. The level-n cylinder sets supply the upper dimension bound; the separated cylinder masses with weights cis​ supply the matching mass-distribution lower bound. Cantor set (C)

Words: 393 Articles: 2
Self-similarity OurBigBook.com
The Cantor set is obtained from [0,1] by repeatedly deleting the open middle third of every remaining interval. Its first stages retain [0,1/3]∪[2/3,1], then four intervals of length 1/9, then eight of length 1/27. After level n, there are 2n retained intervals of length 3−n. The Cantor set is the intersection of all these stages, rather than the set of endpoints visible in any finite drawing.
Equivalently,
C={∑j=1∞​3jaj​​:aj​∈{0,2}}.
(77)
Thus its points admit a base-three expansion using only zero and two. The word “admit” handles numbers with two expansions: 1/3=0.13​=0.02222…3​ is retained as an endpoint. Every infinite binary choice determines a point of C, and differing choices give differing points, so C is uncountable.
Its total retained interval length is (2/3)n→0, so C has zero Lebesgue measure. It is nevertheless nonempty, compact, and uncountable, and has Hausdorff dimension log2/log3: the covers and mass bounds are worked out in Hausdorff dimension of the Cantor set. This separates counting, ordinary length, and fine-scale geometric size in one concrete example.
The self-similarity is exact:
C=31​C ∪ (32​+31​C).
(78)
The Cantor distribution puts half the probability into each copy at every split. It has a continuous cumulative distribution function, the Cantor function, while all its mass lies on a Lebesgue null set. This makes the construction useful in measure theory as well as fractal geometry: it provides a concrete model in which several plausible meanings of “small” disagree.

Words: 115
Cantor set OurBigBook.com
For the middle-third Cantor set C and positive integer d, Cd is compact and totally disconnected. A connected subset projects to a point in each coordinate and is therefore itself a point. At level n, the product has 2dn cubes of side 3−n. These covers give dimension at most dlog2/log3. The product digit probability assigns each cube mass 2−dn; a ball of radius comparable to 3−n meets only a bounded number of cubes, so its mass is at most a constant times rdlog2/log3. The cover-cost argument for Hausdorff dimension proves the matching lower bound. Thus compact totally disconnected Euclidean subsets can have arbitrarily large Hausdorff dimension when the ambient dimension is allowed to increase.

Words: 87
Diffeomorphism OurBigBook.com
On a compact smooth manifold without boundary, every smooth self-map sufficiently C1-close to a diffeomorphism is a diffeomorphism. Reducing to a map near the identity, invertibility of its differential follows uniformly by compactness. It is then a proper local diffeomorphism, hence a finite covering map. Sufficient C0 closeness gives a homotopy to the identity on each component; its induced map on the fundamental group is surjective. The covering therefore has one sheet on each component, proving the assertion. This lets a nearby Lagrangian submanifold transverse to cotangent fibers be represented by a single global differential one-form graph.

Words: 261 Articles: 3
Cobordism OurBigBook.com
Two closed oriented rational Witt spaces are Witt bordant if their signed disjoint union is the collared boundary of a compact oriented Witt space with collared boundary. Disjoint union gives the bordism group ΩnWitt​.

Witt null-bordism in dimensions one two and three

Words: 84
Witt bordism OurBigBook.com
Every odd-dimensional closed oriented Witt space bounds its closed cone: the new vertex has odd-dimensional link, so introduces no Witt obstruction. For a closed oriented two-dimensional pseudomanifold, normalize to a surface, fill each surface component by a handlebody, and attach a collar of the original space using the finite normalization map. Along the singular collar arcs the links are unions of circles; at their interior starting points the links are wedges of two-spheres. These links have zero middle intersection homology, so the construction is a three-dimensional Witt null-bordism.

Words: 148 Articles: 1
Witt bordism OurBigBook.com
For k≥1, the rational middle intersection pairing induces an isomorphism Ω4kWitt​≅W(Q). The restriction k>0 matters: the degree-zero group is Z. In positive dimension congruent to zero modulo four, a space is Witt null-bordant precisely when its middle intersection form is metabolic.
Metabolic intersection form of a four-dimensional product
Words: 103
Witt bordism classification OurBigBook.com
A nontrivial product of positive-dimensional closed oriented Witt spaces of total dimension four has metabolic rational middle intersection form. For dimensions 1+3, the two Künneth summands in degree two pair only with one another, so either is a half-dimensional isotropic subspace. For dimensions 2+2, the outside degree-two summands pair with one another, and the IH1⊗IH1 summand has the tensor pairing of two symplectic forms. A Lagrangian in the first symplectic factor tensored with the entire second factor is a half-dimensional isotropic subspace of that summand. Adding one outside summand gives a Lagrangian in the complete middle form. The Witt bordism classification then makes the product null-bordant.

A compact smooth h-cobordism of dimension at least six between connected simply connected closed manifolds is diffeomorphic to a product, relative to its incoming boundary. The boundary manifolds consequently are diffeomorphic. The dimension and simple-connectivity hypotheses are sufficient conditions, not necessary properties of a product cylinder. The two boundary inclusions being homotopy equivalences are necessary for a trivial cobordism.

An oriented knot cobordism is a compact oriented smooth surface properly embedded in S3×[0,1] with prescribed knots at its incoming and outgoing boundary. A connected genus-zero knot cobordism between knots is a knot concordance. Composing knot cobordisms adds their genera.

Start with (X0​⊔X1​)×[0,1] and attach an (n+1)-dimensional one-handle D1×Dn to one n-ball in each component of its outgoing boundary. The new outgoing boundary is X0​#X1​, so this is a cobordism from X0​⊔X1​ to their connected sum.

Chern-Weil homomorphism

Words: 419 Articles: 9
Geometry and topology OurBigBook.com
Chern-Weil theory constructs closed characteristic forms by applying invariant polynomials to the curvature of a connection.

Pontryagin class (pk​(E)=(−1)kc2k​(E⊗R​C))

Words: 69
Chern-Weil homomorphism OurBigBook.com
For a real vector bundle E, its Pontryagin classes are the even-index Chern classes of its complexification with the displayed alternating signs. They lie in integral cohomology of degrees 4k and obey a total-class product formula under direct sums. If a metric connection on a vector bundle has curvature matrix R, its first real representative is p1​(E)=−tr(R∧R)/(8π2). The Bianchi identity makes this representative closed, and Chern-Weil connection transgression makes its de Rham cohomology class independent of the connection. This normalization gives degree-four A-hat form −p1​/24.

A-hat form (A(R)=det1/2(sinh(R/(4πi))R/(4πi)​))

Words: 80
Chern-Weil homomorphism OurBigBook.com
For the vector-bundle curvature matrix R of a metric connection on a vector bundle on a real oriented vector bundle, the A-hat form is the even differential form defined by the displayed finite-degree power series, with square root having constant term one. The expression is independent of the choice of orthonormal frame. Equivalently, for formal paired curvature Chern roots ±xj​, it is ∏j​(xj​/2)/sinh(xj​/2). The Bianchi identity makes it closed, and changing the connection changes it by an exact differential form via Chern-Weil connection transgression. Its degree-four part is −p1​/24, where p1​=−tr(R∧R)/(8π2) is the first Pontryagin class form.

Chern-Weil connection transgression (∂t​TrFt2​=2dTr(A˙t​∧Ft​))

Words: 48
Chern-Weil homomorphism OurBigBook.com
A variation of the connection one-form has F˙=DA​A˙. The Bianchi identity and graded cyclic matrix trace imply ∂t​Tr(F∧F)=2dTr(A˙∧F). Thus the Chern-Weil theory four-form changes by an exact differential form, and its integral on a closed four-cycle is connection-independent. For a general unitary bundle, include the corresponding trace-product term in the Second Chern form.

Second Chern form OurBigBook.com
The second Chern number is the integral of the second Chern class over an oriented four-cycle. For a suitably normalized SU(n) curvature on a compactified four-manifold, it is an integer.

A Chern-Simons form is an odd-degree transgression form whose exterior derivative is an invariant polynomial in the curvature form. For the trace polynomial of degree k, dω2k−1​=Tr(Fk); the Chern-Simons 3-form is the degree-three case.

Y=8π21​Tr(A∧dA+32​A∧A∧A)

satisfies dY=C2​.
Chern-Simons number of a gauge field (NCS​)
Words: 68
Chern-Simons 3-form OurBigBook.com
For an oriented three-dimensional slice Σ, use the Skew-Hermitian trace convention
NCS​[A]=−8π21​∫Σ​tr(A∧dA+32​A∧A∧A).
(82)
Since the differential of the integrand is tr(F∧F), a space-time slab oriented by dt∧volΣ​ has instanton charge k=NCS​(t+​)−NCS​(t−​) when the side boundary contributes no flux. For a pure gauge A=h−1dh, this reduces to the winding integral (24π2)−1∫Σ​tr(h−1dh)3. Gauge transformations of nonzero winding can shift it by an integer.
Gauge change of the Chern-Simons three-form
Words: 53
Chern-Simons 3-form OurBigBook.com
For an anti-Hermitian SU(N) connection one-form, normalize the Chern-Simons three-form by 1/(8π2) and use Ag=g−1Ag+g−1dg. Its change is −dTr(dgg−1∧A)/(8π2)−Tr(g−1dg)3/(24π2). On a closed three-manifold the first term integrates to zero, while the latter is an integer with the fundamental matrix trace. Hence the integral is defined modulo integers; integer-level exponentials are invariant under large Yang-Mills gauge transformations.

Envelope (mathematics, F(x,y,s)=0,∂s​F(x,y,s)=0)

Words: 49
Geometry and topology OurBigBook.com
A geometric envelope is a curve tangent to the members of a smoothly varying family of curves. For a regular implicit family F(x,y,s)=0, candidate contact points also satisfy the partial derivative condition ∂s​F=0; regularity is needed to turn these candidates into an actual envelope. The Mach cone is a three-dimensional analogue for expanding spheres.

Geometry OurBigBook.com
A measure of separation between locations or objects. In a metric space, distance is specified by a metric satisfying positivity, symmetry and the triangle inequality. The familiar straight-line separation in Euclidean space is Euclidean distance; other metrics can assign different distances to the same pair of points.
